profile.name: Raj Shah
profile.thesis: I build AI agents and automation that run on real enterprise data — and the validation that keeps them correct.
profile.standfirst: Application Developer at Cogent People · Agentic AI & data systems on AWS
profile.bio:
My background is Computer Science and Data Science together, and that combination shaped how I think about building software: an application is only as good as the data feeding it and the evaluation proving it works.

At Cogent People I build AI agents and workflow automation for an enterprise analytics team: multi-step manual reports turned into scripted pipelines, and a multi-agent assistant that answers questions against a governed data warehouse. Most of the job is the unglamorous part — routing, validation, access control, and checking answers against the data instead of trusting the model. Before that, at Boundary Remote Subsurface Solutions, I built ML pipelines for a geospatial AI framework fusing heterogeneous subsurface data, which taught the same lesson in a different domain: data quality and validation decide whether a model is trustworthy, not the model itself.

The projects on this site follow that same thread — a full-stack application, a production-style backend assistant, and a research pipeline built to be evaluated honestly rather than to look impressive.

projects.title: EvacAI
projects.subtitle: AI-powered disaster preparedness platform · IBM Z × UNSA Hackathon
projects.contribution: Built the ML-based risk-scoring model and the backend API integrations — geocoding, live weather, and disaster-alert feeds — that fed the evacuation plan.
projects.problem: During floods, hurricanes, wildfires, and earthquakes, the information people need — weather, active alerts, nearby shelters — is split across separate services, at exactly the moment they have the least capacity to assemble it themselves.
projects.idea: A FastAPI backend that joins geocoding, live weather, disaster alerts, and shelter data into a single per-location query, scores the situation with a risk model, and hands the assembled context to IBM watsonx/Granite to generate a specific evacuation plan — surfaced through both a SwiftUI iOS app and a web client.
projects.engineering: My part was the risk-scoring model and the integration layer underneath it — the services joining geocoding, weather, and alert feeds into one consistent per-location context before it reaches the risk model or the generation step. Getting that join right mattered more than the generation step: watsonx only produces a useful plan if the context underneath it is accurate.
projects.outcome: A working platform — deployed FastAPI backend plus a SwiftUI iOS client — that turns a single location into a risk score and a generated evacuation plan, built in a hackathon timeframe as a 4-person team.

projects.title: RU-PATH
projects.subtitle: Backend assistant for Rutgers parking and transit
projects.problem: Rutgers parking permits, campus zones, and bus routes are scattered across PDFs, department pages, and route tables — and the right answer depends on lot, permit type, time of day, and campus. Students and visitors routinely get it wrong.
projects.idea: Turn that scattered reference material into a conversational assistant: a Flask backend routes each question to the right engine — parking logic or bus routing — using intent detection and fuzzy matching against structured campus data, then hands the resolved context to DeepSeek for a natural-language answer.
architecture: Structured Campus Data — 5 permit types · 6 bus routes · 4 campuses
projects.engineering: The interesting part isn't the language model — it's the routing layer in front of it. Three separate engines (chatbot, parking logic, routing) split across roughly 1,588 lines of Python handle intent detection and resolve a query against structured permit, zone, and route data with fuzzy string matching before anything reaches DeepSeek. That keeps answers grounded in Rutgers' actual rules instead of the model improvising them, without needing a vector database or retrieval framework to do it.
projects.outcome: A working Flask API that resolves parking and transit questions across 4 Rutgers campuses, with the structure of the domain data — not a retrieval pipeline — doing the grounding work.

metrics.label: routing engines — chatbot, parking logic, bus routing
permit types · bus routes · campuses covered

projects.title: FOMC Yield Curve Prediction
projects.subtitle: Understanding how Federal Reserve language moves Treasury markets
projects.problem: Central-bank tone is widely assumed to move rates, and NLP-on-FOMC papers are everywhere. Almost none of them report what the sentiment features are worth against a plain macro baseline, which makes the claimed gains impossible to judge.
projects.idea: Build an NLP and machine-learning pipeline over three decades of FOMC statements, then hold every model to a strict test: does it actually beat a deliberately simple macro-only baseline, once validated the way a time-series problem requires rather than the way that flatters the model?
architecture: NLP Feature Extraction — TF-IDF + Hawkish/Dovish Scoring
projects.engineering: The core engineering decision was the evaluation, not the modeling. Every model was scored against a deliberate 6-feature macro-only baseline across all 9 targets (2Y, 10Y, 2s10s spread × 1-, 3-, 5-day horizons), under walk-forward validation so no model ever saw a future meeting during training. Per-fold RMSE standard deviation was reported rather than averaged away — that's what exposed how much of the claimed gain sits inside the noise band rather than being a real effect.
projects.outcome: The best configuration (Random Forest, 2Y 1-day) reached 8.7 bps RMSE against an 11.0 bps macro baseline — a 21% improvement. Across the other eight targets, gains ranged from 0.8% to 10.6%, and fold-to-fold standard deviation (±4.3 bps) ran roughly double the model differences. The honest reading is that FOMC sentiment adds little over macro features once you validate properly. Reporting that was the point.

metrics.label: bps RMSE — best model vs macro baseline, 2Y 1-day
